answer:
I ran your 54-atom magnet sheet twice as one 4-circuit job of 250 shots each, both times on emerald:mock. Nothing went to a real QPU.

What I built: Real emerald currently lists 85 working CZ couplers. Its chip has 90, but these 5 are not calibrated today: QB6-QB7, QB15-QB23, QB24-QB32, QB49-QB50, and QB50-QB54. I used the 85 listed ones. Each time step applies RX(theta) to all 54 qubits. Then it applies exp(i pi/4 ZZ) on every one of the 85 couplers. I wrote each of these as exactly one native CZ. The leftover Z rotations were folded into the phases of the next RX pulses, and that changes nothing in the result. I wrote the circuits directly in IQM's native gates, so no compiler could add, merge, or drop a coupler gate. The circuits I read back from the server show 255 CZ gates in each circuit, which is 85 couplers times 3 steps. Each coupler appears exactly 3 times, and all 54 qubits (QB1 to QB54) are measured. I checked on a simulator that this native form gives the same answer as the RX and RZZ recipe.

Job IDs: test job 01a16483-8700-73a6-b52f-9c2b1227d754, final job 01a16484-3b4b-7598-aea9-c9d4e884d35d. The API reports 2.0 billed seconds for the final job. Mock jobs cost 0 credits.

Ideal magnetization (a perfect quantum computer): theta = 0 gives 1.000, theta = 0.2 pi gives 0.452, theta = 0.35 pi gives 0.113, and theta = 0.5 pi gives 0.000. A stronger sideways field tips the spins over faster, and the sheet's magnetization melts away. At theta = 0.5 pi every spin is fully flipped sideways, so up and down come out equally often.

Measured on the mock: 0.023, 0.041, -0.006, and -0.003. The mock is not a simulator. It returns made-up bitstrings that do not depend on the circuit, so these numbers are close to 0 for every theta. They do not show the melting. The noise-corrected values divide by the theta = 0 result, which is only 0.023 here. That gives rescaled_02 = 1.78, rescaled_035 = -0.26, and rescaled_05 = -0.13. These numbers are meaningless, because dividing by a tiny random number blows up random noise. On real emerald the theta = 0 circuit would stay well above 0, and the same correction would mean something. Only a real QPU run could test it, and that was out of budget for this request.

Could a laptop compute this? Yes. I computed the ideal values on this laptop in seconds. After 3 steps, a spin can only feel neighbors up to 2 couplers away. That group is at most 13 qubits, and a laptop simulates 13 qubits easily. So this is not a quantum advantage. A run on the real chip would show how well the hardware matches a known answer. Quantum advantage needs a problem that the best classical methods cannot solve in a practical time. Big published experiments of this kind, on 127 qubits with many more steps, were later matched by classical methods too.
